questions.question: What is the difference between a Part-of-Speech (POS) tag and a dependency parse?
options: POS tags label individual words; dependency parses model the relationships between words.
POS tags are for verbs; dependency parses are for nouns.
POS tags are used in transformers; dependency parses are only for classical NLP.
They are different names for the same thing.
questions.explanation: POS tagging is a token-level classification task (noun, verb, etc.), while dependency parsing is a structural task that determines which words modify which (e.g., subject, object, modifier).

questions.question: In the Universal Dependencies (UD) tagset, how many tags are there compared to the Penn Treebank (PTB)?
options: UD has fewer (17) tags and is language-agnostic; PTB is English-specific and more fine-grained.
UD has more tags than PTB.
UD and PTB have the same number of tags.
UD is only for nouns; PTB is for all parts of speech.
questions.explanation: UD was designed for cross-lingual consistency with 17 broad categories. PTB is more fine-grained (36 tags) and specific to the nuances of English grammar (e.g., separating singular vs. plural nouns).

questions.question: What is the 'most-frequent-tag' baseline accuracy typically found on the Brown corpus?
questions.explanation: Simply assigning the most common tag seen in training for each word achieves about 85% accuracy, serving as a lower bound for more complex POS tagging models.

questions.question: Why is dependency parsing often preferred over constituency parsing in modern NLP?
options: It generalizes better across different languages, including those with free word order.
It is much slower but more accurate.
It produces a flat list instead of a tree.
questions.explanation: Dependency parses represent the relationship between words directly, which is more robust for languages where word order is flexible compared to the rigid phrase-structure trees of constituency parsing.
